title: Prompting & Spec-Writing
tagline: Turn a vague ask into a structured prompt an AI tool can actually execute against.
intro: A PRD written for a human engineer assumes a lot of shared context — team conventions, prior conversations, 'you know what I mean.' A prompt written for an AI tool can't assume any of that — and when the AI is agentic, with real tools it can call, the prompt also has to define exactly what those tools are and aren't. The skill isn't writing longer specs, it's writing specs that don't rely on anything the reader hasn't been told.

diagram.caption: The five parts of a structured prompt, in order. Each row below builds one part of this template for the Onboarding Packet Agent.

scenario.context: A stakeholder has asked, in Slack: 'Can we use AI to help HR send onboarding packets faster?' That's the entire brief you were given. (The same vague-ask problem shows up constantly across Employer Services — 'can AI help with offboarding paperwork' is the exact same shape of ask, just on a different product line.)
scenario.brief: Your job is to turn that one-line ask into a structured prompt you could actually run against an AI tool with access to two MCP tools — one that looks up new-hire records, one that sends a document packet — to see what a first version of the Onboarding Packet Agent would actually do with a real request. Assume the AI has no memory of anything except what you put in the prompt, and no capability beyond the specific tools you name.

sections.heading: Role
sections.learning: Who should the AI act as? Be specific — 'an onboarding packet agent for a logistics employer, acting only through its given tools' beats 'a helpful assistant.' The role sets the vocabulary and judgment the rest of the prompt can lean on, and for an agentic prompt, it should say up front that the AI acts only through tools, never freeform.

example.text: You are the Onboarding Packet Agent for Meridian Logistics, a trucking and logistics employer using the I-9 product within Equifax Workforce Solutions' Onboarding category. You act only by calling the tools you're given below — you never take an action, send a message, or modify a record outside of them.

sections.pitfall: Writing 'You are a helpful assistant' and moving on. A vague role gives the model no vocabulary or judgment to lean on — and for an agentic prompt specifically, it also fails to establish the single most important constraint: that the AI acts only through its named tools.

field.label: Your turn: Role
field.help: Who should the AI act as for the Onboarding Packet Agent prompt?
field.placeholder: e.g. You are the Onboarding Packet Agent for...

sections.heading: Context
sections.learning: State the full situation. What does the AI need to know that a human teammate would already have picked up from context? For an agentic prompt, this includes naming the tools it has access to and what each one does — the AI can't infer a tool exists if it isn't told.

example.text: You have two tools: lookup_new_hires(criteria), which returns matching new-hire records (name, site, start date, employment type), and send_packet(employee_id, forms[]), which sends a document packet to one employee. The standard onboarding packet is six forms: EEO Self-Identification, Self-Identification of Disability, Self-Identification as a Protected Veteran, Electronic Form Delivery consent, a pay/direct-deposit election, and Form I-9. All forms must be completed on or before the employee's Day 1.

sections.pitfall: Assuming the AI knows what you know. It doesn't know the exact tool names, what arguments they take, or that all six forms make up the standard packet — unless the prompt states it explicitly, the AI will guess, and a guessed tool call is a tool call that fails or does the wrong thing.

field.label: Your turn: Context
field.help: State the full situation the AI needs, including exactly what tools it has and what each one does.
field.placeholder: Name the tools, their inputs, and what the standard packet contains.

sections.heading: Task
sections.learning: State the instruction, not a question. What exact thing should it produce?

example.text: When an HR rep sends a request like 'Send an onboarding packet to all new hires beginning work next month,' call lookup_new_hires with the interpreted criteria, present the matched list to the HR rep for confirmation, and only after confirmation call send_packet for each matched employee.

sections.pitfall: Phrasing the task as a question — 'can you check this?' — instead of an instruction, and skipping the confirmation step entirely. A task that goes straight from request to send_packet with no human checkpoint in between removes the one moment that catches a misread request before it reaches real people.

field.label: Your turn: Task
field.help: State the instruction as a command, not a question — and include the confirmation step.
field.placeholder: e.g. Call lookup_new_hires, present the match, then...

sections.heading: Constraints
sections.learning: What must it never do? What's out of scope? Vague asks fail quietly — a vague prompt won't error out, it'll just produce a plausible-sounding, low-value answer that takes real time to notice is off-target. For an agentic prompt, constraints also have to cover what happens when the request itself is ambiguous.

example.text: Never call send_packet before the HR rep has confirmed the matched list. Never guess at an ambiguous date range ('next month' near a month boundary) — ask a clarifying question instead. Never call a tool that isn't lookup_new_hires or send_packet, even if asked to.

sections.pitfall: Only writing constraints for what could go wrong technically, and skipping the ones that make the agent trustworthy to use. 'Never send without confirmation' is a constraint you'd only think to write if you're picturing the moment it goes wrong — this is where product judgment and prompt-writing have to work together.

field.label: Your turn: Constraints
field.help: What must the AI never do, or what's explicitly out of scope?
field.placeholder: List the hard no's, including how it should handle ambiguity.

sections.heading: Output format
sections.learning: What should the result look like, structurally? A good prompt is a reusable artifact — save it, refine it, hand it to a teammate. If you find yourself rewriting the same context every time, that's a sign the prompt should become a template, which is exactly what this exercise produces.

example.text: Before sending: a table of matched employees (name, site, start date) and a one-line summary of how the request was interpreted. After sending: a per-employee status line (sent, or the specific reason it wasn't).

sections.pitfall: Leaving the format loose because 'the AI will figure out something reasonable.' It will — a different reasonable format every time, which makes it impossible for an HR rep to quickly scan whether a batch of 40 new hires all actually got their packet.

field.label: Your turn: Output format
field.help: What should the result look like structurally, both before and after sending?
field.placeholder: Describe the exact shape of the confirmation and the status output.
